name: Puebla
summary_text: Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people; trans women constituted 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year, across at least 17 states reporting victims. Its legal-gender-recognition law (2021) keeps an 18-year minimum-age requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, yet the state congress has still not corrected the text — legislative non-compliance with a final court ruling is itself a hostility signal directly relevant to a visitor whose documents must match presentation. There is no dedicated investigative machinery, no transfeminicide offence, and no state-level enforcement data. The combination of top-of-table lethality and open defiance of the judiciary distinguishes Puebla from states that simply lack statutes: here a statute exists but the legislature actively refuses to conform it to a binding ruling. Context for comparison: Mexico City, which also had high counts in 2024-25, created a transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocol within months; Estado de México, which likewise defies a Supreme Court ruling on recognition, has at least had a penal-code hate-crime provision covering bias motives since 2021. Puebla has neither the court-compliant text nor any criminal-law protection or enforcement innovation.

sources.title: Concentran mujeres trans 58% de los asesinatos a personas LGBT+ en 2025 - Quadratín Michoacán
sources.claim_summary: Quadratín (June 2026), citing NGO observatory data: trans women concentrated 58.3 percent of the killings of LGBT+ people recorded in Mexico during 2025; at least 17 states reported victims; Puebla headed the 2025 state table with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people.

sources.title: Gender Recognition in Mexico by State | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch feature on state gender-recognition laws in Mexico (March 2025): Puebla enacted its legal gender recognition law in 2021 but with an 18-year age requirement the Supreme Court declared unconstitutional in March 2022; the state congress has not amended the text since; the feature maps which of the 32 states had (and had not) legislated a recognition procedure by March 2025, and links document mismatch to police questioning risk for trans people.
